rel_path: Non-sequential\Coherence Interference and Diffraction\Interference Example 1- A Simple Interferometer.ZMX
name: Simple Interferometer.
note: Note the 50% coating on the front faces of the beam splitter plates. A He-Ne laser beam is split at the first splitter and recombined by the second splitter. One of the mirrors is at a slight angle wi th respect to the second, and so the beams are recombined with some tilt. The coherent sum of the ray amplitudes shows the interference fringes between the two beams. ZEMAX can model any form of shearing interferometer using this technique. Note that the total power is cons erved between incohernet and coherent additions, but that the peak irradiance of the coherent beam is 2x that of the incoherent beam sum, as it should be.

rel_path: Non-sequential\Coherence Interference and Diffraction\Interference Example 3- Coherence Length Reduces Fringe Visibility.ZMX
filename: Interference Example 3- Coherence Length Reduces Fringe Visibility.ZMX
name: Coherence length sample
note: Note the difference in coherence length for the two sources (double-click on the source objects and look at the Sources tab). A small tilt angle between the two sources causes interference. Observe the coherent irradiance at several distances from the source. As the propagation length approaches the coherence length, the interference fringes wash out.

rel_path: Non-sequential\Coherence Interference and Diffraction\Interference Example 4- Diffraction Limited Imaging.ZMX
name: A laser focussing system demonstrating diffraction
note: This system is a well optimized lens producing a diffraction-limited spot. Detector object 5 is looking at the incoherent addition of the rays landing, and so sees an infinitesimal point (in fact, it is limited to the size of the central pixel). Detector object 6 is the coherent data for each pixel as the Huygens integral of all rays incident upon the detector, resulting in the diffraction Point Spread Function. The ring structure and diffrac tion-limited width can be clearly seen. See http://www.zemax.com/support/knowledgebase/what-is-a-ray for more details.

name: Two color mixing gives white
note: In this example, two monochromatic wavelengths, .460 microns and .570 microns are mixed together with equal power. These correspond to blue and yellow, and when mixed together  yield a white color. These wavelengths are commonly produced by 'white' LEDs.

name: Black Body light dispersed by a grating
note: Look at the properties of the Source Ellipse object to see it is set as a blackbody radiator at a temperature of 5000 degrees, and we generate rays at 100 wavelengths in the range .3 to .9 microns. This is greater than the visible region, and so a Detector Color set to True Color (photometric) response will see only that part that the human eye will respond to. The same detector set to show Fals e Color in the Detector Viewer will show the radiometric data. Both radiometric and photometric data are recorded by the Detector Color. Note also that rays outside the visible are drawn as black when rays are colored by the apparent visible color.

name: Ray Splitting and Colorimetry
note: A grating splits a blackbody source into +1, 0 and -1 diffraction orders. The undiffracted light is white, and the +/- 1 orders  are dispersed to either side of it. We trace one million rays from the source, and because of the splitting at the grating 3 million rays land on the detector.

You can see the shadow cast by the wineglass, and note that in some parts of the shadow the light is dispersed into yellow and blue. The number in x, y and z is user defined, as are the separations between the objects and the angles between objects. ZEMAX will optionally draw the whole array of lenses, a bounding box that contains the array (useful when there are many objects in the array) or both, for the most convenient display of data. You can make arrays of any object, including Boolean and CAD objects. The advantage of using array objects is that they use far less memory and trace faster than an equivalent number of individual obj ects.

rel_path: Sequential\Image Simulation\Example 2, Double Gauss Experimental Arrangement.ZMX
name: Double Gauss Experimental Arrangement
note: A double-Gauss lens was optimized with the object at infinity and with the field of view defined in angles. This example shows a typical experimental arrangement in which a source scene is modeled usi ng a bitmap to represent a test chart, and the light from that scene is collimated using an auxiliary optical system. This allows spatial frequencies in the object plane to be defined in cycles/mm, an d for the resulting contrast to be measured in the image plane. Note the darkening of the image towards the corners.

rel_path: Sequential\Image Simulation\Example 3, A blue notch filter.ZMX
name: A Blue notch-filter
note: The glass plate has a coating that rejects the blue wavelength region. As a result, the blue circle is not passed by the system. Note the 'Use Polarization' flag in the Settings dialog of the Image Si mulation feature must be on for the coating to be accounted for. As this design has no aberrations, the PSF grid is computed using a delta function. This is faster than computing the geometric or diffraction psf which is unnecessary as the design uses only a paraxi al lens.

rel_path: Sequential\Image Simulation\Example 4, a diffraction limited system.ZMX
name: Imaging through the Hubble Space Telescope
note: In this file we image a simple object though the HST. The input scene subtends only 0.001 degrees field of view. Note that the Geometric Image Analysis feature predicts a sharp image, because geometri c calculations predict unphysically good imaging in diffraction limited systems, but the Image Simulation correctly shows the blurring due to the finite passband of the optical system. Note also that the input scene is oversampled so that the resulting pixels are comparable to the size of the PSFs in the grid.

name: Resolution variation over the field of view
note: This example uses the same lens as example 2, but in this case a small (5mm) source scene consisting of four grids of lines is moved vertically in the field of view. The effects of lateral color and s agittal/tangential MTF can be clearly seen. Note that at each field point the detector is centered on the field of view of interest. Alternatively, the detector can be defined to be a single large detector that stays at the same position as the image is moved. Use the 'Reference' control in the detector settings to define exactly what you want. Maximize or zoom into each window to see the full resolution image.

name: Focal Plane Blurring and Keystone Distortion
note: Configuration 1 is diffraction limited across its field of view. The PSF grid may need to be maximized for its details to be visible. Configuration 2 shows both image and object surfaces tilted (use c ontrol-A to switch configurations). ZEMAX automatically switches from diffraction to Geometric PSF calculation when the spot is 20x the diffraction limit. This is done independently for each field and wavelength. Note that the central x -slice is still diffraction limited, while the top and bottom x-slices are geometrically aberrated.

name: Apochromatic prism
note: The merit function shows how the chief-ray angle over wavelength is targeted. The prism tilt angles are optimized to provide apochromatic performance. A final chief-ray angle solve locates the image s urface normal to the primary wavelength chief ray. File contributed by Eddie Judd.

name: THREE GLASS DESIGN SUGGESTED BY D. BUCHROEDER
Apochromatic Objective designed by Barry Johnson
note: My motivation was in rewriting the chapter in the Lens Design Fundamentals book on design of spherically corrected achromat, Kingslake had mentioned the difficulty of eliminating the large spherochrom atism characteristic of an apochromat, even with an air gap. I decided to make the gap into more of an "air lens" and was pleased with the results. The "trick" was to drive the marginal chromatic to zero rather than the zonal. I also force tertiary spherical to come into play with the primary and secondary. I didn't play around to see how fast I could make it, but f/8 is not so bad. The positive and negative peaks of the zonal aberration for the e line are balanced while they vary for the other colors.

name: Gaussian Quadrature over Wavelengths
note: This lens has been optimized with a reasonable merit function and constraints using three equally weighted wavelengths over the visible. In the Wavelength Dialog, choose to use four Gaussian-Quadrature weighted wavelengths over the same range, and rebuild the merit function keeping the same boundary conditions. Re-optimize and note the improvement in performance. Note that we have not added any extra variables, aspherics etc...this improvement comes simply from the wavelength selection and the relative weights of the selected wavelengths!

name: Gaussian Quadraure over an Annular pupil
note: This telescope is artificially unobstructed to show that the four rays in the merit function compute the same RMS wavefront error as the 256x256 grid of rays in the Wavefront Map. Now add a 25mm obscuration to surface 2, and note that the Wavefront Map RMS error changes, but the merit function does not. This is why GQ could not be previously used in systems with obscured pupils . Rebuild the merit function and set the OBSCURATION parameter to .333 You will see that ZEMAX traces a different four rays, in the unobscured region of the pupil, and that the merit function again equa ls the RMS as seen by the 256x256 grid of rays!
